<reason>Both sides ran coherent, adaptive cases with real comparative weighing, but CON (A) controlled the decisive clash. A's dilemma — either the worker truly refuses (reviving the hostile-courier problem) or a platform-adjudicated review means "the worker refuses nothing" — was pressed from the opening through the closing, and PRO's answers never dissolved the core tension of indicting a decade of platform bad faith while handing that same platform the gatekey. PRO's best move, the B4.5 jujitsu ("if the star can't be trusted to punish, it can't be a mandatory foundation"), was rhetorically sharp but conflated direct punishment with post-investigation use, a distinction A's tripwire/accumulation answer (A4.1) had already drawn and B never squarely rebutted. A also won the auditability exchange (published rating distributions vs. discretionary volume-denials) and the safety-signal point. B scored with the "landmine" reframe, the restaurant-complaint analogy against the scarlet letter, and direct A1/A2 answers. Minor costs on both sides: A slightly distorted B's grant-case in A4.5; B mislabeled a reference and overclaimed a total concession. Clipping hit both roughly evenly. Net: clear but competitive win for CON.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Rebuttal 2 (A4.1–A4.5): answering B's pressure questions with the "tripwire vs. response" distinction, then flipping B's own A1/A2 answers into a dilemma — "refusal that changes nothing, or concealment that misleads everyone" — which forced B onto the defensive for the rest of the debate.</best_rebuttal>
